claim.pdf_says: ACCEPT Format 2 (temporal): 'DATE [ YYYYMMDD ]' with BOTH DATE and YYYYMMDD underlined, and 'DAY [ YYYYDDD ]' with BOTH DAY and YYYYDDD underlined (verified on the enlarged crop -- each of YYYYMMDD and YYYYDDD carries its own underline rule inside the brackets).
claim.why_it_matters: YYYYMMDD and YYYYDDD are required (reserved) words inside their optional brackets. Every other word in this same figure -- ACCEPT, FROM, DATE, DAY, DAY-OF-WEEK, TIME, END-ACCEPT -- is wrapped in \underline, so the omission is not a stylistic choice; it reads as if YYYYMMDD/YYYYDDD were user-supplied operands rather than fixed reserved words, which would let an implementor accept any word there.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED against both sources at high magnification. PDF (E:/Temp/specrecon/v606/spec_p606.png, 300 dpi, crop enlarged 5x to E:/Temp/specrecon/v606/crop_date_line.png): the Format 2 (temporal) brace group prints four alternatives. On the first line I see two distinct, separated underline rules -- one running under 'DATE' and terminating before the '[', and a second, independent rule beginning after the '[' and running under 'YYYYMMDD' only, terminating before the ']'. The brackets themselves are NOT underlined. The second line is identical in structure: a rule under 'DAY', a gap, then a separate rule under 'YYYYDDD' inside unmarked brackets. 'DAY-OF-WEEK' and 'TIME' each carry a rule as well. There is no ambiguity and no OCR/rendering artifact -- the gap between the DATE rule and the YYYYMMDD rule is several glyph-widths wide and both rules sit on the same baseline offset as every other underline in the figure. MARKDOWN (specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 25254, byte-identical to the work-unit page-606.md line 39): '\underline{\text{DATE}} \text{ [ YYYYMMDD ]} \\ \underline{\text{DAY}} \text{ [ YYYYDDD ]}' -- YYYYMMDD and YYYYDDD sit in plain \text{} with no \underline wrapper, while ACCEPT, FROM, DATE, DAY, DAY-OF-WEEK, TIME and END-ACCEPT in the very same formula are each wrapped in \underline. The claim quotes both sources accurately. REFUTATION ATTEMPTS, ALL FAILED: (a) the words are not merely reflowed or moved -- they are present, only their underlining is dropped, and underlining is normative typography here, not decoration; (b) there is no compensating figure-note block -- I read lines 25240-25270 and the formula is followed immediately by 'Format 3 (screen):' with no '> Figure notes' paragraph, unlike the many figures elsewhere in this transcription that do carry such notes and explicitly enumerate which words are underlined; (c) this is not the transcription's own house style for optional-word marking, since the transcription elsewhere goes out of its way to flag genuinely non-underlined words ('PRINTING is not underlined', 'AS is not underlined', 'ON is not underlined'); (d) it is not a harmless formatting difference, because the meaning is fixed by the standard's own notation rules. NORMATIVE IMPACT: 5.2.2 Keywords -- 'Keywords are reserved words or context-sensitive words. They are shown in uppercase and underlined in general formats. They are required in order to select the functionality associated with that keyword.' 5.2.3 Optional words -- 'Optional words ... are shown in uppercase and not underlined in general formats. They may be written to add clarity.' Stripping the underline therefore does not make YYYYMMDD look like an operand (5.2.4 fixes operands as LOWERCASE); it demotes a keyword to an OPTIONAL/noise word -- one that may be written or omitted with no effect on functionality. That directly contradicts 14.9.1.3 general rules 7 and 8 in the same transcription, which make DATE without the YYYYMMDD phrase a six-digit item and DATE with the YYYYMMDD phrase an eight-digit item. An implementor working from the markdown figure alone would treat 'ACCEPT x FROM DATE YYYYMMDD' as equivalent to 'ACCEPT x FROM DATE' and return YYMMDD where YYYYMMDD is required. The words are also listed in the 8.10 context-sensitive word table ('YYYYDDD | ACCEPT statement', 'YYYYMMDD | ACCEPT statement'), which is only coherent if they are keywords selecting functionality.
verdict.corrected_description: REAL, but the stated harm is misdiagnosed. The typographic facts are exactly as claimed: in the printed Format 2 (temporal) figure on page 606, YYYYMMDD and YYYYDDD each carry their own underline rule inside their brackets (the brackets are unmarked), and the markdown at specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 25254 renders both as plain \text{} with no \underline while underlining every other uppercase word in the same formula. Two corrections to the rationale: (1) YYYYMMDD and YYYYDDD are CONTEXT-SENSITIVE words (8.10 table, both mapped to 'ACCEPT statement'), not plain reserved words. (2) Dropping the underline does not make them read as user-supplied operands and would not 'let an implementor accept any word there' -- 5.2.4 fixes operands as LOWERCASE, so an uppercase non-underlined word reads unambiguously as an OPTIONAL WORD under 5.2.3, i.e. a noise word that 'may be written to add clarity' with no functional effect. That is the actual and more damaging misreading: it makes 'ACCEPT x FROM DATE YYYYMMDD' appear semantically identical to 'ACCEPT x FROM DATE', contradicting 14.9.1.3 general rules 7 and 8 (six-digit DATE without the phrase, eight-digit DATE with it) and the corresponding YYYYDDD rules for DAY. Fix: wrap both words in \underline inside their brackets -- '\underline{\text{DATE}} \text{ [ } \underline{\text{YYYYMMDD}} \text{ ]}' and '\underline{\text{DAY}} \text{ [ } \underline{\text{YYYYDDD}} \text{ ]}' -- leaving the brackets themselves unmarked, as printed.
